readme.html:
Coral

One MCP server for every service your agents use, with your credentials and your rules. Agents write short TypeScript programs. Coral runs them in a sandbox, adds the credentials, and checks every call against your policy.

Why Coral

Connecting an agent to many services usually means many MCP servers, a token pasted into each one, and every tool definition loaded into every prompt. Coral replaces that with one server:

  • Smaller context, fewer round trips. The agent searches for the tools it needs instead of loading them all up front. It then sends one program that can call several tools and return only the fields the answer needs.
  • Agents build on what already worked. When a program works, the agent saves it as a function. The next time, it calls that function in one step instead of finding the tools and writing the program again. Saved functions are typed and appear in search alongside provider tools.
  • Agents never hold credentials. Coral stores your tokens and adds them to each call. Programs run in an isolated sandbox with no secrets, no network access, and no imports.
  • You decide what runs. Set each tool to allowed, approval required, or disabled. A call that needs approval waits until a person approves it.
  • Every run is recorded. Review each program and the calls it made in the Coral UI.
  • You host it. Run Coral on your laptop or on your own server. Your data, credentials, and usage history stay with you.

Coral includes setup recipes for GitHub, Linear, Jira, Notion, Gmail, Stripe, Datadog, Sentry, HubSpot, and more. You can add any service that has an OpenAPI document or an MCP server.

Get started

  1. Install Coral. Download the desktop app for macOS, Linux, or Windows from the releases page, or run a shared server for your team.

  2. Add a provider. A provider is one service your agents can use. Pick one from the catalog, or bring your own OpenAPI document or MCP server. See Add a provider.

  3. Connect your agent. Each workspace in Coral has its own MCP URL. Copy it from the Coral UI and add it to your MCP client:

    claude mcp add --scope user --transport http coral <your-mcp-url>   # Claude Code
codex mcp add coral --url <your-mcp-url>                            # Codex

    For Cursor, VS Code, OpenCode, and other clients, see Connect an MCP client.

Now ask your agent something that needs that provider, such as "What are my open pull requests?"

Setup guides and the configuration reference are at withcoral.com/docs.

How Coral works

graph LR
    Agent["Your agent"] -->|"search, exec"| MCP["Coral MCP server"]
    You["You"] -->|"providers, policy, approvals"| UI["Coral UI"]

    subgraph Coral["Coral (your machine or server)"]
        MCP --> Run["Sandboxed program run"]
        UI --> Gate["Credentials and policy"]
        Run --> Gate
    end

    Gate --> GH["GitHub"]
    Gate --> SL["Slack"]
    Gate --> Own["Your OpenAPI or MCP service"]

The agent searches for the tools it can use and reads their TypeScript signatures. Then it sends Coral a short program. This one finds open pull requests that have no reviewer and posts them to Slack:

const { data: pulls } = await coral.providers.github.pulls.list({
    owner: "withcoral",
    repo: "coral",
    state: "open",
});

const unreviewed = pulls.filter((pull) => pull.requested_reviewers.length === 0);

await coral.providers.slack.chat.postMessage({
    channel: "#engineering",
    text: unreviewed.map((pull) => `#${pull.number} ${pull.title}`).join("\n"),
});

return unreviewed.map((pull) => pull.number);

Coral adds the credentials and checks each call against your policy. If posting to Slack requires approval, the run pauses there until you approve it. Only the pull request numbers go back to the agent, not the full GitHub response. Once this works, the agent can save it as a function, and later programs call it as coral.functions.<name>().

To learn about providers, accounts, policy, and workspaces, read Concepts.

Upgrade from Coral 0.x

Coral 1.0 replaces the SQL interface with TypeScript programs. It is a rewrite and starts from fresh state: it does not convert what 0.x stored, and it tells you at startup if it finds 0.x state. See Upgrade from Coral 0.x.

Development

To run Coral from a checkout, follow the development guide.

Community

Ask questions, share ideas, and show what you built in our Discord or on GitHub issues.

Security

Do not report security issues in public issues or pull requests. See SECURITY.md.
